title: High-C Foster, stock arrangements and verses
summary: Phillips remembers the high C as a novelty in the 1920s, and says stock arrangements were cut up and tunes then had verses.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Some can and some can't. See, I remember the time when I was coming along and first started playing trumpet, they had a cat out there they called "High-C Foster." He played High-C and they thought that was great. That's what they called him, because he played... He didn't play no Jazz.
Where was he from? Where did he play?

He was from Cleveland. But he played in the show bands, like circus bands. [SINGS]...He played up around C, you know what I mean. So that was high... When you played C in those days, you were playing high, man. Cats said, "Man, that cat played high C." Like, they'd write an arrangement. In them days there wasn't too many arrangements. They had what they...
What days you are talking about now?

In the 20's. Yeah, in the 20's and the 30's. In the 30's is when they just started to playing arrangements. They used to play a lot of stocks, and take the stock and cut it up -- cut this part off, and put that part in there, and maybe they'd make a modulation and go to the last chorus. If they wanted to play that middle part and make a modulation and go the last chorus and play something. Playing that sometimes... Many of them didn't sound so good, the middle of... You know, the stocks. They don't make them that way no more now. See, when I came on, they wrote verses and everything to the stock. All they give you right now is the chords. They wrote verses. All tunes that was written then had verses. All of them. Like "Them There Eyes" and all them tunes. [SINGS IT] -- that's the verse.
